cards.explanation: The answer is True. Esther, the queen, has no summons and walks into that court anyway. The text says that as soon as the king saw her standing there, "…she found favor in his sight." (Esther 5:2) Going in unsummoned could mean death (Esther 4:11), so finding favor in his sight is exactly what she needs in that moment.

The answer is scepter, friends. The king holds out the gold scepter in his hand, and Esther comes forward and touches its tip (Esther 5:2). It's the king's signal that she can come closer. I'd have touched that thing with my whole mustache.

The answer is up to half the kingdom, bakers. The king asks, "What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you." (Esther 5:3) He says it right there in the court, to Esther. Half a kingdom is quite an offer.

The answer is the king and Haman at her banquet today, friends. Esther says, "If it pleases the king, may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king." (Esther 5:4) Haman is the king's top official, the one who promised money to destroy the Jews (Esther 3:9). The king can give her half a kingdom, and she asks for a dinner guest list.

The answer is False, bakers. The king doesn't say to take it slow. He says, "Hurry," and commands, "and bring Haman, so we can do as Esther has requested." (Esther 5:5) When a king says "Hurry," I'd be moving faster than a cookie sheet out of a hot oven.

The answer is to come back tomorrow for another banquet, friends. Esther says, "…may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them. Then I will answer the king’s question." (Esther 5:8) The king has asked twice, and she still holds her answer for one more day. I think the king's patience is being tested here.

The answer is that he doesn't rise or tremble, bakers. The text says Mordecai, Esther's cousin (Esther 2:7), "…did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence." (Esther 5:9) Haman was walking out full of joy, and Mordecai just stays put. I think it was a very quiet kind of standoff.

The answer is rage, friends. The text says Haman "…was filled with rage toward Mordecai." (Esther 5:9) One minute he's glad of heart, and the next he's full of rage. That's a fast drop, like a cookie sliding off the cooling rack.

The answer is False, friends. The text says, "Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home." (Esther 5:10) He's full of rage, but he holds it in and leaves the gate. Holding it in is not the same as letting it go, and I think Haman is still carrying it.

The answer is that only he joined the king at Esther's banquet, bakers. Haman tells them, "Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king." (Esther 5:12) Haman lists it with his wealth, his sons and his promotions. I think he'd have put it on a banner if he'd had the time.

The answer is False, friends. Haman says, "Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate." (Esther 5:13) He just listed all that wealth and honor, and it still isn't enough for him. One man sitting at a gate is spoiling the whole batch for Haman.

The answer is a gallows fifty cubits high, friends, and I think this one hurts. Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his friends tell him, "Have them build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it." (Esther 5:14) It's a heavy verse. Mordecai is the one the plan is aimed at.

The answer is True, bakers. After the gallows advice, Zeresh and his friends add, "Then go to the banquet with the king and enjoy yourself." (Esther 5:14) They hand Haman the plan and tell him to enjoy himself. The banquet is still on the calendar.
